section.title: Remember Your Creator
section.sectionRationale: This is the emotional climax of the Teacher's counsel. Light is sweet, so rejoice in every year, yet remember the days of darkness and the coming judgment. Then, in one of the most beautiful poems in Scripture, he urges the young to remember their Creator before old age and death dismantle the body, before the dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God. The whole movement lands on the refrain that has run through the book: everything under the sun is fleeting.
section.thesis: Enjoy the gift of life while knowing it is brief and accountable to God, and above all remember your Creator now, in youth, before the body fails and the spirit returns to the God who gave it.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to rejoice in life yet remember darkness and judgment; the poem urging you to remember your Creator before old age and death take the body apart and the spirit returns to God; and the closing refrain, futility of futilities, everything is fleeting.

units.label: Rejoice, yet remember judgment
units.note: light is sweet, but life is brief

verses.text: Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun.
So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all. But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. Everything to come is {{hevel|futile}}.

Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment.
So banish sorrow from your heart, and cast off pain from your body, for youth and vigor are {{hevel|fleeting}}.

units.label: Remember your Creator before the end
units.note: the poem of aging and death

verses.text: Remember your {{bara|Creator}} in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come and the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,”
before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain,
on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop, when those grinding cease because they are few and those watching through windows see dimly,
when the doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades away, when one rises at the sound of a bird and all the daughters of song grow faint,

when men fear the heights and dangers of the road, when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring, and the caper berry shrivels, for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets.
Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed, before the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well,
before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the {{ruach|spirit}} returns to God who gave it.
“Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher. “Everything is {{hevel|futile}}!”

hevel.gloss: Vapor, breath, mist; the anchor word of Ecclesiastes, rendered futile, fleeting, or meaningless. It names how everything under the sun slips through the fingers, here the passing of youth and vigor and of all that is to come. The word does not deny that life is good, but insists it is breath-brief, and so drives the reader to the God who is not fleeting.

bara.gloss: To create, the verb of Genesis 1, used only of God's making. Remember your Creator, literally your Creators, a plural of majesty for the one God who formed you. To remember Him is not merely to recall a fact but to know, honor, and live toward the God who made you, before the years come when you cannot.

ruach.gloss: Wind, breath, spirit. At death the dust returns to the ground and the ruach returns to God who gave it, an echo of Genesis 2:7, where God breathed life into the man. Life is a loan of breath from God, and it goes back to Him; this is why remembering the Creator now is the one thing that matters.

basic.context: This is the tender heart of the book's ending. Life in the light is genuinely sweet, so the Teacher says: enjoy it, all of it, every year you are given. But keep two things in view. The days of darkness will be many, and God will bring everything you do into judgment. Then he speaks to the young especially: remember your Creator now, while you still can, before old age comes. In a haunting poem he pictures the aging body as a great house falling into disrepair, hands trembling, eyes dimming, teeth few, until the silver cord snaps and death comes. The dust goes back to the ground and the breath of life goes back to God who gave it. And over it all the old refrain sounds again: everything under the sun is breath-brief.
basic.hermeneutics: The famous poem in chapter twelve is read in different ways. Many take its images as an allegory of the body breaking down in old age, the keepers of the house as trembling arms, the grinders as failing teeth, the windows as dimming eyes. Others hear it more as a picture of a household and estate collapsing, or of a gathering storm and funeral. Either way the meaning is plain: the body wears out, death comes, and the wise remember their Creator before it does. Verse seven, the spirit returning to God, is not yet the full New Testament hope of resurrection, but it confesses that our breath is a loan from God that returns to Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The refrain word is hevel, breath or vapor, here saying that youth and vigor and all that is to come are fleeting. Remember your Creator uses bara, the verb reserved for God's own making in Genesis 1. And at death the ruach, the breath or spirit, returns to God who gave it, echoing the moment in Genesis when God breathed life into the dust.
basic.typology: The dust returning to the ground recalls the sentence of Genesis 3, and the spirit returning to God who gave it looks for an answer beyond the grave. That answer is Christ, who took our dust, died, and rose, turning the return to the ground into a seed of resurrection. The Creator we are told to remember in youth is the same Word by whom all things were made, now made flesh.
basic.christ: We are told to remember our Creator, and the New Testament tells us that all things were created through Christ and for Him. In Him the God who gave us breath became flesh, entered our aging, dying world, and was made subject to futility to redeem it. His resurrection is the reason the dust returning to the ground is not the end; the body that fails will be raised. To remember the Creator in the days of your youth is, this side of the cross, to come to know God now through Christ.
basic.god: God is the Creator who gives us breath and to whom that breath returns, and He is the Judge who will bring every deed into account. He is not distant from our enjoyment; light and life are His good gifts to be received with gladness. Yet He is holy, and the sweetness of life is meant to lead us to Him, not away from Him.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2:7 and 3:19 stand behind the dust and the breath. Ecclesiastes 3 says God has set eternity in our hearts. Second Corinthians 5 speaks of the earthly tent taken down. Romans 8 says creation was subjected to futility in hope, and John 1 and Colossians 1 name Christ as the Creator.
basic.oneStory: The book's honest verdict, that life under the sun is fleeting, does not end in despair but in a summons: remember your Creator now. That call reaches its answer in Christ, the Creator who entered our dying and rose, so that the breath which returns to God returns to a Father who raises the dead.

context.literary:
The passage runs from 11:7 to 12:8 and is built as one long sentence of instruction followed by one long poem, joined by the word 'remember.' The first part, 11:7 to 10, is a pair of commands about joy that bracket a warning. 'Rejoice' appears in verse 8 for the old and verse 9 for the young, and the warning 'know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment' sits at the centre of verse 9. The unit ends in verse 10 by returning to joy with the reason, that youth is fleeting.

Then the grammar changes. In 12:1 the main verb is 'Remember,' and everything after it hangs on a chain of 'before' clauses. Before the days of adversity, 12:1. Before the light is darkened, 12:2. Before the silver cord snaps, 12:6. Before the dust returns, 12:7. The sentence does not reach its main clause until the end, so the reader is carried through the whole decline before being told what to do with it. The effect is deliberate: the poem enacts time running out.

The imagery moves in three waves. Verses 2 to 5 are an extended scene of a house and a landscape growing quiet, with servants trembling, women at the mill stopping, windows dimming, doors shutting, and birdsong fading. Verse 5 turns to nature, the almond blossoming, the grasshopper dragging, and ends with the funeral: 'man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets.' Verse 6 gives four broken vessels, a cord, a bowl, a pitcher and a wheel, each an image of a life-giving thing coming apart. Verse 7 gives the plain statement behind the images.

Verse 8 is the inclusio. 'Futility of futilities,' says the Teacher, is the book's opening cry in 1:2 almost word for word. The Teacher speaks in the third person here, as in 1:2, so the poem is framed by his name. In the larger structure, 11:7 to 12:8 completes the movement that began with the commands of 11:1 to 6: since you cannot know the future, act now and enjoy now, and since the end is certain, remember the Creator now.
context.historical:
The poem draws on the physical world of a village household. The 'keepers of the house' and the 'strong men' suggest a household with servants and guards, the 'grinders' recall women at the hand mill, the 'windows' were small openings in a wall, and the 'doors to the street' belong to a town. The 'sound of the mill' was one of the sounds of ordinary life, and its silence is a sign of a house that is empty. When Jeremiah wants to picture the end of normal life in a land, he says that the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp will cease, and in the same way these images mark a household winding down.

The almond tree is the first tree to flower in Israel, in the cold of late winter, with white blossoms on bare branches, which makes it a natural picture of white hair. Jeremiah's call vision of an almond branch, Jeremiah 1:11, shows how familiar the tree was. The caper berry is often said to have been used in antiquity to stir the appetite, so if it 'shrivels' it may mean that appetite has failed, though the word is uncertain and older English versions read it as 'desire shall fail.'

Funerals are in view in verse 5. The 'eternal home' is a phrase for the grave, as in Psalm 49:11, where the dead have 'graves as their eternal homes,' and 'mourners walk the streets' recalls the professional wailers of the ancient Near East. The silver cord, the golden bowl and the pitcher at the spring were ordinary objects of lamp, water and well, and their breaking turns daily provision into loss.

For Israel, youth was the time of strength and training. The psalmist could say 'You have taught me from my youth,' Psalm 71:17, and Lamentations says 'It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young,' Lamentations 3:27. The teacher who addresses 'young man' here is speaking in the tradition of wisdom instruction aimed at the next generation, as in Proverbs.
context.canonical:
The passage is written in conversation with Genesis. The 'dust' that returns 'to the ground from which it came' is Genesis 3:19, where God told the man, 'For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.' The 'spirit' that 'returns to God who gave it' is an echo of the creation of man in Genesis 2:7, where God breathed the breath of life into the dust. In the Teacher's poem, Genesis 2 and 3 are played in reverse: the breath goes back, and the dust goes back.

Elsewhere the Old Testament says the same. 'If He were to set His heart to it and withdraw His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust,' Job 34:14-15. 'When You take away their breath, they die and return to dust. When You send Your Spirit, they are created,' Psalm 104:29-30. The Teacher has asked in 3:21, 'Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward?' and in 12:7 he gives the one thing he is sure of: the spirit goes back to God.

The call to remember has a long history. Israel was commanded to remember the Sabbath, Exodus 20:8, and to 'remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth,' Deuteronomy 8:18. To remember in Scripture is to act toward someone in faithful loyalty, not just to recall them. The phrase 'God will bring every deed into judgment,' in 11:9, returns at the close of the book in 12:14.

In the New Testament the passage meets fulfilment on every side. Paul says that 'though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day,' and that the earthly tent will be replaced by 'an eternal house in heaven,' 2 Corinthians 4:16 and 5:1. Jesus commits His spirit to the Father, Luke 23:46, and Stephen asks Him to receive his own, Acts 7:59. The resurrection answers the poem: what is sown perishable is raised imperishable, 1 Corinthians 15:42.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher is making an appeal to the young, and he is doing it with unusual care. He does not begin with a warning. He begins with a blessing: light is sweet, so enjoy it. He then names the cost of not remembering, and the cost is not guilt but loss. A person who waits until the years of 'no pleasure' to turn to the Creator has put off the one thing that would have made all the years rich.

He wants the young to hear two things together that they would prefer to keep apart. Joy is good, and judgment is certain. A young man may be tempted to treat these as enemies, so that to take God seriously is to give up delight. The Teacher says that they belong together. The gladness of youth is a gift of the Creator and so is best received by those who remember Him.

He also wants the old to hear their own story told honestly. The poem of chapter 12 is not cruel; it is loving. It names what is coming without sentimentality, so that the hearer is prepared. And it ends, not in the grave, but in God: the breath goes back to the one who gave it. The whole poem moves toward that sentence, and the hearer is meant to move with it. The call is to a relationship now, with the one who made us, before the years that make everything harder.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem of 12:2 to 7 describes. It is a picture of ageing and death and is not a command to feel any particular way about them. The commands are the ones that frame it: rejoice, banish sorrow, remember your Creator. Those are prescriptive, and they are addressed first to the young but are good for anyone.

Care is needed with 'walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes,' 11:9. It is a permission but not a licence, and the next clause qualifies it with judgment. The permission is to enjoy the good things God gives, as in the rest of the book. It is not a call to follow every impulse, and Numbers 15:39 shows how Israel was told not to follow their own hearts and eyes into rebellion. The verse needs the clause that follows it.

'Banish sorrow' is likewise not a command never to grieve. The same book says that sorrow has its use, 7:3, and Jesus blesses those who mourn. It is advice to a young person not to waste the days of strength in needless vexation, and to put away what poisons them.

For readers now, the poem of ageing is not a prediction every person will fulfil in detail. Some die young and some age more gently. The point is the sound of its warning: you will not always have the strength you have now, so do not put off the turn to God. And the statement of 12:7, that the spirit goes back to God, is a statement about where life comes from, and it is not yet the full hope of the resurrection, which the rest of Scripture supplies.

debates.question: Is the poem of 12:1-7 an allegory of the ageing body, or a broader picture of a house, a storm and a funeral?

views.label: An allegory of the body
views.case: Read item by item, the poem maps onto the ageing body: the keepers of the house are the trembling arms, the strong men the bowed legs, the grinders the few remaining teeth, those at the windows the dimming eyes, the daughters of song the failing voice and hearing. The almond blossom is white hair and the shrivelled desire the loss of appetite. This reading is ancient and widely held.

views.label: A picture of a household and a storm
views.case: Others notice that the images do not fit the body neatly. The darkened light, the returning clouds and the shut doors read as a gathering storm and a house shutting up, and the mourners in the streets make a funeral. On this view the poem paints the end of a life as a scene, and every detail is not a code.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: The poem may blend the two: a house in decline is a picture of a body in decline, and a funeral procession is a picture of its end. Poetry can use images that are partly bodily and partly scenic without forcing every phrase onto a single meaning.

debates.bearing: All views agree on the summons that leads the poem, 'Remember your Creator,' and on the plain fact of verse 7. The reader does not need to decode every image to hear the warning, and an over-confident allegory runs the risk of missing the poem's feel, which is a slowing and a hush.

debates.question: What does it mean that 'the spirit returns to God who gave it' (12:7)?

views.label: The life-breath goes back to its Giver
views.case: The verse echoes Genesis 2:7 and Job 34:14-15 and Psalm 104:29, where God gives and takes breath. On this reading it says that life comes from God and returns to God at death, and it says no more than that. It is a statement of ownership and not of personal survival.

views.label: The person goes to God for account
views.case: Because the book ends with judgment, 12:14, and because 11:9 says God will bring the young man into judgment, the return of the spirit is read as the person's passage into God's presence, to be accounted for. This is how many Christian readers take it, in light of Luke 23:46.

views.label: An answer to the question of 3:21
views.case: In 3:21 the Teacher asked, 'Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward?' In 12:7 he states what he knows: the spirit goes to God. The earlier question was about whether humans differ from beasts; here the answer is that the spirit returns to the Giver, which is a more open and hopeful word.

debates.bearing: The verse stops short of describing what happens next, and it should not be pressed into a full doctrine of the afterlife. But it plainly teaches that death is not the end of dependence on God. The breath was a loan and goes back to Him, and that is enough to ground the call to remember Him now.

debates.question: Is 'walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes' (11:9) sincere or ironic?

views.label: A sincere permission
views.case: The surrounding verses command joy, and the Teacher elsewhere commends enjoyment of life as God's gift, 9:7-9. The permission is real: the young are meant to relish their strength and their days.

views.label: A mild irony
views.case: Numbers 15:39 warns Israel against following their own hearts and eyes, and some interpreters hear the Teacher's words as ironic, letting the young follow their desires only to be struck by the clause 'know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment.'

debates.bearing: The text carries a real invitation and a real limit. It is better to hold both: the young are free to rejoice, and the one who gives joy will ask what was done with it. Whether read as irony or permission, the verse is not a rule to follow impulse.

study.originalLanguages:
The key verb of the passage, 'remember,' zakar, is more than a mental act. In the Old Testament it describes faithful action toward someone. God 'remembered Noah' and sent a wind over the earth, Genesis 8:1. Israel is told to 'remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy,' Exodus 20:8, and to remember that God gives power to gain wealth, Deuteronomy 8:18. To remember your Creator is to give Him His place in the living of your days. The word returns in 12:6 as 'Remember Him,' and it answers the earlier sorrow that 'no one remembered' the poor man, 9:15, and that the dead are forgotten. In a book full of forgetting, the Creator is the one to be remembered.

The word translated 'Creator' is a participle of the verb bara, 'to create,' and it is the word used of God as the Creator of the ends of the earth in Isaiah 40:28. In the Hebrew text of 12:1 it takes a plural form, which many take as a plural of majesty, like the form of the word Elohim, God. The participle describes a continuing identity: He is the one who creates, and so He is the one with the claim on a life.

'Judgment' in 11:9 is mishpat, and the verb of 'bring' is the same one that closes the book in 12:14, 'God will bring every deed into judgment.' The two verses form a pair at the start and the end of the final movement, so the call to enjoy is bracketed by the call to answer.

In 11:10 the 'sorrow' that is to be banished is ka'as, vexation or grief, and it is the same word the Teacher praised in 7:3, 'Sorrow is better than laughter.' The apparent contradiction is a matter of season. There is a sorrow that makes the heart wise and a vexation that wastes the days of youth, and the Teacher knows the difference. The BSB renders the hevel of verses 8 and 10 as 'futile' in one place and 'fleeting' in the other, and the footnote at verse 10 gives 'or futile.' The word means a breath, and both senses fit.

In 12:7 the two verbs are the same: the dust 'returns,' shuv, to the ground and the spirit 'returns,' shuv, to God. A single verb carries both movements, so that the end of a person is a double return. And the spirit goes back to 'God who gave it,' from natan, the same verb used for God giving the days of life in 9:9 and the gifts of 5:18. Everything we have was given, and it is therefore returned.

The word for 'eternal home,' beit olam, in 12:5 uses olam, long or lasting time, and shows that the grave was thought of as a lasting dwelling. The ruach of 12:7 is the same word that meant wind in 11:5, and the Hebrew keeps the two chapters tied to each other.

typology.type: The spirit that returns to God who gave it, 12:7
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher's last sentence on the end of life is lived out by Jesus. On the cross He cried, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, taking words from Psalm 31:5, and Stephen followed Him with 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,' Acts 7:59. The type is carried further: for Jesus the return was not the end, since the Father raised Him, Romans 8:11. The Teacher says that the spirit returns to God; the gospel says that the body will follow, 1 Corinthians 15:42-44. The type falls short in saying nothing of a risen body.

typology.type: The house that falls into ruin, 12:3-5
typology.fulfillment: The body as a dwelling that wears out is picked up by Paul: 'if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven,' 2 Corinthians 5:1. The decay of the house is not final, since it is replaced by a better one, 'so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life,' 5:4. And outwardly wasting, 'yet our inner self is being renewed day by day,' 2 Corinthians 4:16. The type falls short because the Teacher sees only the collapse, while Paul sees a rebuilding that follows it.

The poem begins its decline by the darkening of sun, moon and stars. At the cross, 'darkness came over all the land,' and 'the sun was darkened,' Luke 23:44-45. It is an echo and not a declared fulfilment, but the Gospels show the true Light entering the days of darkness for us. He said 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness,' John 8:12. The darkened light of the poem is answered by a light that was put out for three hours and then rose.

typology.type: The pitcher shattered at the spring, 12:6
typology.fulfillment: Vessels that draw life from a spring and then break are a picture of a life cut off from its source. God calls Himself 'the fountain of living water,' Jeremiah 2:13, and Jesus offers the thirsty a fount 'springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14, and says 'Streams of living water will flow from within him,' John 7:38. This is an echo, since the Gospels do not quote the poem, but the pairing is natural. The type falls short in that the Teacher's spring is where the pitcher breaks, while Christ's is where the cup is filled.

To remember the Creator is, in the New Testament, to know Him in the Son, through whom 'all things were created,' Colossians 1:16, and who is the radiance of God's glory, Hebrews 1:2-3. At His table He gave His people a new act of remembering: 'do this in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19. The Creator remembered in youth is the Redeemer remembered in bread and cup. The type is carried forward, not replaced, since remembering the One who made us now includes remembering the One who died for us.

study.christ:
The opening command, 'Remember your Creator,' leads at once to the Son, for the New Testament says that 'all things were created through Him and for Him,' Colossians 1:16, and that God made the universe through Him, Hebrews 1:2. The Creator the Teacher tells the young to remember is the same one who came into the world He made, and the invitation to remember Him in youth is, after the incarnation, an invitation to know Him by name. Jesus says to the people, 'Come to Me,' and the call to the young is the call to come to Him while they have strength.

It leads to Him through the judgment of 11:9. 'For all these things God will bring you to judgment' becomes, in the New Testament, a statement about the Son. The Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22, and God has appointed a day to judge the world 'by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31. The judge is also the one who died for those He will judge, which changes what judgment means. For those in Christ, the day of reckoning is not a terror, because the one who sits in judgment has already taken the penalty, John 5:24.

It leads to Him through the poem's end. The Teacher can say that dust returns to the ground and the spirit to God. What he cannot say is what comes next. Christ answers this in His own death. He committed His spirit into the Father's hands, Luke 23:46, and then He was raised. The ageing and breaking of the body in verses 3 to 5 is answered by His resurrection body, 'sown perishable... raised imperishable,' 1 Corinthians 15:42, and by the promise that the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus will give life to our mortal bodies, Romans 8:11. The poem's final return is not a final defeat.

It leads to Him through joy. The Teacher says 'rejoice,' and Jesus says, 'I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete,' John 15:11. The call to banish sorrow from a young heart is met by the one who gives a new heart, Ezekiel 36:26. He does not cancel the days of darkness; He enters them, for 'darkness came over all the land' while He hung on the cross, Matthew 27:45, and He comes out on the other side with a light that does not go out.

Finally, the passage names the futility of everything under the sun, and Christ is the one who bore it. Creation 'was subjected to futility... in hope,' Romans 8:20, and the hope is Him. A caution is needed: the silver cord, the pitcher and the wheel are not hidden images of the crucifixion, and the poem does not mention a Messiah. The links come from the way the New Testament takes up the poem's themes: the Creator, the return of the spirit, the earthly house, and the judgment. The Teacher's poem needs the gospel to be finished.
study.god:
The passage presents God first as Creator and Giver. 'Remember your Creator' makes Him the origin of every youth and every day, and 'the spirit returns to God who gave it' makes Him the source of every life. The word 'gave' is the same one used of the days of life in 9:9 and of enjoyment in 5:18. A God who gives is also a God who owns, and the claim He has is the claim of one who has made us and sustains us. When He takes away their breath, creatures die and return to dust, Psalm 104:29, and Job says that if He withdrew His Spirit and breath 'all flesh would perish together,' Job 34:14-15. Our life is a loan and not a possession.

He is generous with light. 'Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun,' 11:7. The God of this passage does not resent human happiness. The Teacher says to rejoice in all the years and to be glad in youth. The fear of God that closes the book does not conflict with that. It guides it. A God who wanted His creatures to be joyless would not have made the sun to please the eyes.

He is the Judge who sees. 'God will bring you to judgment,' 11:9, and the verb is the same as the one in 12:14, 'God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing.' This is not a threat to dampen joy but an expression of His justice, because a world in which nothing is ever weighed would be a world where nothing matters. The New Testament adds that all must appear before Christ, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and that it is appointed to die once and then to face judgment, Hebrews 9:27.

He is faithful to the old as well as the young. 'Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray. I have made you, and I will carry you,' Isaiah 46:4. And the psalmist, taught from his youth, prays 'Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God,' Psalm 71:17-18. The poem of ageing is therefore not a poem about God's absence. The God who is to be remembered in youth is the one who carries us to our grey hairs.

He is above futility and yet not careless of it. The Teacher's closing refrain says that everything is breath, and Paul says the creation was subjected to futility by God 'in hope,' Romans 8:20. The God of this passage is not trapped by the fleetingness He has ordained; He rules it, and He promises to redeem it.

For worship, the passage asks for gratitude in youth and trust in age. It calls us to fear and rejoice together, to receive each year as a gift, and to give the last year back to the one who gave the first.

crossReferences.note: God formed man from the dust and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils. Ecclesiastes 12:7 reverses this, with the dust going back and the breath going back. Genesis 2:7 uses a different word for breath, neshamah, but the picture is the same: life is a gift that God puts in and takes back.

'For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.' Ecclesiastes 12:7 quotes the sentence in a way, taking the judgment pronounced after the fall and showing it lived out in every ageing body. The decline of the poem is Genesis 3 in slow motion.

If God withdrew His Spirit and breath, 'all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust.' It supports the reading of Ecclesiastes 12:7 as a statement of God's ownership of life, and it ties spirit and dust together just as the Teacher does.

'When You take away their breath, they die and return to dust. When You send Your Spirit, they are created.' The psalm sets death and creation in the same hand of God. It shows that the Teacher's return of breath is not a mere end, since the same Spirit can renew the face of the earth.

Israel is told to wear tassels to remember the commandments and not to follow their own hearts and eyes. It is the closest echo of the 'ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes' in Ecclesiastes 11:9, and it explains why the Teacher adds a clause about judgment.

The length of our days is seventy years, or eighty, and the psalmist prays 'teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.' It is the same reckoning that drives Ecclesiastes 11:8 and 12:1, and the prayer asks God to give the wisdom that the Teacher urges.

The psalmist says, 'You have taught me from my youth,' and prays that God will not forsake him in old age. It is a living example of remembering the Creator in youth and being kept by Him in old age, which is the pattern that Ecclesiastes 12:1 commends.

'Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray.' The God who made us carries us. It answers the fear in the poem of Ecclesiastes 12 by showing that the years of decline are not years without a Helper.

Paul says that though the outer self is wasting away the inner self is renewed daily, and that the earthly tent will be replaced by an eternal house. It takes the poem's image of a failing house and gives it an answer: the collapse is not the end of the building.

'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.' Jesus, quoting Psalm 31:5, makes the spirit's return to God into an act of trust. It shows how the last sentence of Ecclesiastes 12:7 can be prayed, and it is followed by the resurrection.

God 'commands all people everywhere to repent' because He has set a day to judge the world by the Man He appointed, and proved it by raising Him. It gives the judgment of Ecclesiastes 11:9 a name and a pledge, and it is the reason the call to remember the Creator is urgent.

Creation was subjected to futility in hope of being set free from decay. It is Paul's reading of the hevel of Ecclesiastes 12:8. The futility is real, but it is not the last word, since it was imposed 'in hope' and will end in 'the glorious freedom of the children of God.'

study.oneStory:
The poem of Ecclesiastes 12 is the sentence of Genesis 3 heard at the end of a long life. God made the man from the dust and breathed life into him, Genesis 2:7, and after the fall He said that to dust he would return, Genesis 3:19. Every human life in the Bible lives between those two verses. The Teacher takes that long fact and turns it into a call, not to despair but to remember, and to remember in youth.

The call has a place in the story of Israel. The prophets and the psalmists repeated it again and again, 'remember the LORD your God,' and the failure to remember was the root of Israel's long wandering. The Teacher's contribution is to bring it to the individual, the young person at the start of his days, and to tie it to the one thing no one escapes. Everyone will face the days of darkness, and the only question is whether the Creator is known when they come.

The story reaches its centre when the Creator enters the poem. The Word through whom all things were made, John 1:3, became flesh, grew from a child to a man, and took the dust of human life on Himself. He entered the days of darkness, and the cord was cut, the bowl broken, the dust returned. But He was raised, and so the sentence of Genesis 3 is not the last word. 'As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive,' 1 Corinthians 15:22. The spirit that goes back to God goes back to a Father who raises the dead.

For those who are in Christ the ageing body is the tent being taken down while the inner self is renewed, 2 Corinthians 4:16-5:1. The fear and the joy of the passage are held together in the church's own life: she rejoices in the gifts of her Creator and she waits for the judge who is also her Saviour, Acts 17:31.

The end of the story answers each line of the poem. The light that is darkened is replaced by a city that has no need of sun or moon, Revelation 21:23, and 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The mourners no longer walk the streets. The spring does not run dry, for the water of life flows from the throne, Revelation 22:1. And the Creator who was to be remembered in youth is seen face to face. The Teacher's last word, that everything is breath, is answered by the God who makes all things new, Revelation 21:5.

quiz.q: What two things is the young person told to keep in view while rejoicing in life?

options.text: The many days of darkness to come and that God will bring every deed to judgment.
options.note: Joy is real, but held soberly under the shadow of death and the reality of judgment.

options.text: That life is short and that God is watching what we do.
options.note: A fair summary, though the text names the days of darkness and the coming judgment specifically.

options.text: That pleasure is sinful and should be avoided.
options.note: The Teacher commands rejoicing; he does not condemn enjoyment itself.

options.text: That nothing we do matters at all.
options.note: The judgment means our deeds matter deeply, not that they are meaningless.

quiz.q: What is the central command of the poem in chapter 12?

options.text: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before old age and death come.
options.note: The whole poem hangs on this summons to remember God now, while you can.

options.text: Turn to God before your body starts to fail.
options.note: Close to the point, though the text stresses remembering the Creator specifically, and doing so in youth.

options.text: Fear growing old, because life ends in nothing.
options.note: The poem faces death honestly but calls for remembering God, not mere dread.

options.text: Enjoy youth now because God will not judge you.
options.note: The passage explicitly warns that God will bring you to judgment.

quiz.q: What does verse 7 say happens at death?

options.text: The dust returns to the ground, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
options.note: Life is a loan of breath from God that goes back to Him, echoing Genesis 2:7.

options.text: The body goes back to the earth while breath returns to its Giver.
options.note: A faithful paraphrase, though the exact language of dust and spirit and God who gave it is the point.

options.text: The soul simply ceases to exist forever.
options.note: The verse says the spirit returns to God, not that it is annihilated.

options.text: The person is immediately rewarded in heaven.
options.note: The verse does not describe reward; it confesses that breath returns to God.

quiz.q: How should we understand the images of trembling keepers, dimming windows, and a snapped silver cord?

options.text: They picture the body and life breaking down as death approaches, driving us to remember God now.
options.note: Whether read as the aging body or a failing house, the images point to death and the call to remember the Creator.

options.text: They vividly describe the decline that comes with old age.
options.note: True, and the poem uses that decline to press the summons to remember God before it is too late.

options.text: They are random poetic pictures with no clear meaning.
options.note: The images are carefully chosen to portray death's approach.

options.text: They promise that the body will never really fail.
options.note: The poem describes exactly the opposite, the failing of the body unto death.

quiz.q: How does remembering the Creator connect to Christ?

options.text: All things were created through Christ, who entered our dying and rose, so the breath returning to God returns to a Father who raises the dead.
options.note: Christ is the Creator we are to remember and the ground of resurrection hope beyond 12:7.

options.text: Jesus is the Creator through whom all things were made.
options.note: True, and the answer should reach His entering death and rising to defeat it.

options.text: The poem has nothing to do with Christ.
options.note: The New Testament names Christ as the Creator and the answer to death's futility.

options.text: It teaches that Christ keeps believers from ever growing old or dying.
options.note: The hope is resurrection beyond death, not escape from aging in this life.

quiz.q: What does the refrain futility of futilities mean here?

options.text: Everything under the sun is breath-brief and slips away, which is why we must anchor in the God who is not fleeting.
options.note: Hevel names life's vapor-like brevity and drives us to the Creator.

options.text: Life passes quickly and cannot be held onto.
options.note: Right about brevity, though the refrain is meant to push us toward God, not merely to lament.

options.text: Life is worthless and not worth living.
options.note: Hevel means fleeting, not worthless; the Teacher still commands us to rejoice in life.

options.text: Nothing God does has any purpose.
options.note: The futility is of life under the sun apart from God, not of God's own work.

questions: The Teacher says light is sweet and calls you to rejoice in every year. Where do you need to receive life as a good gift rather than take it for granted?
Enjoy your life, he says, but know that God will bring every deed to judgment. How does holding both together, real joy and real accountability, change how you live this week?
Remember your Creator in the days of your youth. Whatever your age, what would it mean to turn to God now rather than putting Him off for a season that may never come?
The poem faces the failing of the body and the certainty of death honestly. What does it stir in you to sit with the truth that your breath is a loan that returns to God?
Christ entered our dust, died, and rose so that the grave is not the end. How does the hope of resurrection reshape the way you face aging, loss, and your own mortality?

translationNotes.note: Everything to come is futile translates hevel, breath or vapor; some editions render it futile or fleeting, naming the brevity rather than the worthlessness of life.
Creator is literally Creators, a plural of majesty for the one God, from bara, the verb used only of God's making in Genesis 1; to remember Him is to know and honor Him, not merely to recall a fact.
The spirit that returns to God renders ruach, wind, breath, or spirit; the line echoes Genesis 2:7, confessing that the breath of life is a loan from God that goes back to Him.
Futility of futilities forms a bookend with 1:2; the Hebrew hevel of hevels is a superlative, this is the most fleeting of fleeting things, everything is vapor.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Ecclesiastes 11:7-10 (chapter 11) and 12:1-8 (chapter 12); chapter field set per verse. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse.
